subtype: Approach: adds buffer days before a deadline [Thinking]
passage:
Asif: project is due on the 15th, we have loads of time 😎
Wasim: I'm aiming to finish by the 10th
Asif: why so early?
Wasim: last term the print shop had a power cut the day before, and half our group had fever that week
Asif: hmm ok that's true
Wasim: so the 10th is my real deadline. the 11th to 14th are for printing, fixing the mess and anything that goes wrong
Asif: fair. what needs doing first?
Wasim: charts by the 6th, writing by the 9th, then on the 10th we read it all once
Asif: 👍 fine, I'll take the charts
Wasim: thanks. if it all goes smoothly we get four days off 🙂

qa.q: By which date does Wasim aim to finish?
qa.a: Wasim aims to finish by the 10th.

qa.q: What is Wasim worried about that makes an early finish sensible?
qa.a: Wasim worries that printing problems or illness could cause delays, as happened last term.

qa.q: What else could Wasim and Asif do to protect the deadline?
qa.a: They could save the work in two places and find a second print shop, so that one closure does not stop them.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt at first about finishing early?
qa.a: Asif might have found it unnecessary and a bit pushy at first, before agreeing after hearing the reasons.

grounding: Shows a student aiming to finish days before the due date because printing and illness often cause delays.

subtype: Approach: keeps some money aside in a monthly budget for surprises [Action]
passage:
Gargi's allowance arrived on the first of every month, and by the third week last term it had always run out. This month she sat on the sofa of the flat she shared and split it in her notebook into columns: rent share, food, bus pass, phone recharge. Then she drew a fifth column and wrote "oops" on top.

"What's that?" asked Darshan from the doorway.

"A small bit I don't touch," said Gargi. "For things I can't plan."

On the twelfth her bicycle chain snapped outside the library, and the repair shop wanted more than she had in her pocket. She took the money from the oops column, paid, and rode home. The food column stayed untouched. She noted the amount in her book and began refilling the column the following week.

qa.q: What did Gargi write on top of the fifth column?
qa.a: Gargi wrote "oops" on top of the fifth column.

qa.q: How did Gargi probably feel when the chain snapped?
qa.a: Gargi was probably startled and a little worried, but not panicked, since the oops column already covered the repair.

qa.q: What could Gargi do if the oops column runs empty early in the month?
qa.a: Gargi could trim a flexible column such as the phone recharge for that month, and refill the oops column when she can.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the fifth column?
qa.a: Darshan might find it curious at first, and after the repair see it as sensible, since it avoided a scramble.

grounding: Shows a student on an allowance keeping a small part aside for an unplanned repair so that one surprise does not empty the month.

subtype: Approach: pads every task so heavily that work expands to fill it [Pitfall]
passage:
Subject: what I found on the Q2 estimates

Hi Payal,

You asked why the Q2 launch was late again, so I went through the tracker. When I made the estimates, I put a big cushion on every task, so each one had ten days for what is really four days of work. The team relaxed. Nobody started early, and most tasks were touched for the first time in the last two days before their dates. Testing came at the very end and squeezed everything. The days I padded never turned into spare days. I believed the padding would keep everyone calm, but calm turned into slow.

Can we talk on Monday about what a better estimate could look like?

Gurpreet

qa.q: How many days did each task get for what was really four days of work?
qa.a: Each task had ten days for what is really four days of work.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet expect the padding to do?
qa.a: Gurpreet expected the padding to keep everyone calm, but the calm turned into slowness.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet do instead of padding every task?
qa.a: Gurpreet could keep honest estimates for each task and hold one shared cushion near the end for real delays, so tasks do not stretch to fill their days.

qa.q: How might Payal feel on reading this email?
qa.a: Payal, who asked why the launch was late again, may feel relieved to get a clear answer, and perhaps frustrated that the launch slipped.

grounding: Shows a heavy cushion added to every estimate, so the team relaxes and still finishes at the last minute.

subtype: Approach: keeps one shared buffer at the end of the project [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Zeenat opened the plan for the app update and deleted the cushions from each task. "Honest numbers only," she told the team. At the bottom she added one bar labelled Buffer, six days, just before the client date. Tarun frowned. "What if my task runs over?" "Then tell me, and we look together," said Zeenat.

Thursday, week three. Tarun's login task took two days longer than planned because the test server crashed. He said so at stand-up. The team took two days from the buffer, and every other task kept its date.

Friday, week five. The update went out with four days of buffer left. Zeenat wrote in the notes: buffer used once, for a real delay.

qa.q: How many days of buffer were left when the update went out?
qa.a: Four days of buffer were left when the update went out.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling on Monday when he asked what if his task runs over?
qa.a: Tarun felt uneasy about being caught short or blamed for an overrun, now that the padding was gone.

qa.q: What could the team do if the buffer were used up early?
qa.a: They could talk to the client about scope or dates as soon as possible and drop the least important item, instead of hiding the delay.

qa.q: How might the client see the update going out with buffer left?
qa.a: The client might see the team as reliable, having received the update before the agreed date.

grounding: Shows a team removing padding from tasks and holding one shared buffer before the deadline, used only for a real delay.

subtype: Approach: builds a simple version first and improves it [Action]
passage: Yuvan's model house was due at the end of the week, and he had a big plan: windows, a balcony, a garden, blue paint. On Monday, after school in the art room, he made just a plain box from a cereal carton with a flat cardboard roof glued on top. It looked a bit bare. "Show it to Rajni Ma'am anyway," he told himself. She turned it around slowly. "Steady work. The roof sits straight. What comes next?" Yuvan pointed at the empty walls. "Windows." On Tuesday he cut four windows. On Wednesday he painted the walls yellow. By Friday a small balcony stood at the front, and the house was done, with every step already checked.

qa.q: What did Yuvan make first?
qa.a: Yuvan first made a plain box with a flat cardboard roof glued on top.

qa.q: How did Yuvan feel about the first plain box?
qa.a: Yuvan felt it looked a bit bare and may have been unsure, but he showed it to the teacher anyway.

qa.q: What could Yuvan do if the teacher suggested a different roof shape?
qa.a: Yuvan could change the roof early while the model is still simple, which is easier than fixing it after the paint is done.

qa.q: How might Rajni see Yuvan's early showing?
qa.a: Rajni may be pleased that Yuvan asked early, since comments can shape the model while it is easy to change.

grounding: Shows a boy building a plain box house with a roof, showing his teacher, then adding windows and paint on later days.

subtype: Approach: releases a small first version and asks users for feedback [Action]
passage: I'm Sonali, and last month I did something I had never done: I sent out an app before it was ready. I used to dream of two hundred questions, a leaderboard and cartoon levels. Then Seema said in class, "Just show us something." So I put in ten questions and sent the link to eleven classmates. I did not ask anything. I just watched the results. Nearly everyone skipped the two history questions and played all three cricket ones twice. That told me more than any guess of mine. So the next weekend I wrote fifteen more cricket questions and left history alone. I am still a little embarrassed about how plain the first version looked. But I am glad I sent it.

qa.q: How many questions were in the first version?
qa.a: The first version had ten questions.

qa.q: How does Sonali feel looking back at the first version?
qa.a: Sonali feels a little embarrassed about how plain it looked, but glad it was sent out.

qa.q: What else could Sonali do to learn what classmates like?
qa.a: Sonali could ask two or three classmates to say aloud what they would change while they play, along with watching which questions get skipped.

qa.q: How might Seema see the app now?
qa.a: Seema, who asked to be shown something, may be pleased to have played it and might like that the cricket topic grew.

grounding: Shows a teenager releasing ten questions first, watching what classmates skip and adding more of the popular topic.

subtype: Approach: decides the smallest useful version and defers extras [Thinking]
passage:
Mentor note, Friday demo prep. The campus notes team came in with a list of nine features. Indu wrote them on the board and asked the others one question: "With only two weeks, what does a student need on day one to bring a friend back?" Answers came out loud. "Somewhere to upload notes." "A way to find them." Someone asked about ratings, and Indu said, "Nice, but nobody rates what they cannot find yet." Profiles went the same way. The board ended with two lines under Launch and seven under Later, and the team spent the rest of the hour dividing upload and search between them. I said nothing during the reasoning and only asked when they would show it to a first-year student. They said Tuesday.

Tanuja, project mentor

qa.q: How many lines ended up under Launch and under Later?
qa.a: The board ended with two lines under Launch and seven under Later.

qa.q: What did Indu want the team to think about?
qa.a: Indu wanted the team to think about what a student needs on day one, so they would focus on what brings a friend back.

qa.q: What could the team do if first-year students ask for ratings?
qa.a: The team could move ratings up the Later list once real requests show that it matters.

qa.q: How might a first-year student see a site with only upload and search?
qa.a: A first-year student might find it simple and useful straight away, since finding notes is the main need.

grounding: Shows a student team choosing the smallest useful launch, upload and search, and postponing other features.

subtype: Approach: ships something too thin to be useful and learns little [Pitfall]
passage: Arohi here. I was one of eight testers Bhupen invited last Saturday for the language-swap app. The idea: pair two people who each speak what the other wants to learn, for a weekly call. What we got was a sign-up screen and a profile form that crashed twice. No pairing, no call, nothing to try. We spent forty minutes telling Bhupen about the missing "forgot password" link, the tiny letters and a button that did nothing. Not one of us could say whether we would want a partner. Bhupen took notes quickly, smiling, and said, "Great, very helpful." I can't say if that was true. I left with a page of comments about basics and no answer to the only question that mattered.

qa.q: How many testers did Bhupen invite?
qa.a: Arohi was one of eight testers Bhupen invited.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt hearing only comments about basics?
qa.a: Bhupen may have felt disappointed or defensive, though the smile and the words "very helpful" hide it, so Arohi cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do next to learn whether the idea has value?
qa.a: Bhupen could set up even a simple hand-made pairing and one real call, so testers can try the core idea, and then ask whether they would use it again.

qa.q: How did the testers see the session?
qa.a: The testers, including Arohi, felt they could not judge the idea since there was nothing to try, and left with comments only about basics.

grounding: Shows a founder releasing a version too bare to test the core idea, so feedback is only about missing basics.

subtype: Approach: revises the minimum to include the core value and repeats short cycles [Revision]
passage:
In the incubator's meeting room, Disha read the survey scores aloud. "Weak. People said nice list and never came back."

Ritu had built a tool-sharing app for her colony whose first version only listed who owned what. She looked at the results for a long while. "Nobody could ask for a drill. That was the whole point." She opened her laptop and added one button: Borrow tonight. Then she set up two-week cycles: release on Monday, watch what forty residents actually tap for ten days, meet on the second Friday and change something.

In the first cycle, most taps landed on drills and ladders, and almost nobody opened the profile page. Ritu deleted the profile page and moved ladders to the top.

Disha nodded. "That's evidence, not opinion."

qa.q: What one button did Ritu add?
qa.a: Ritu added one button: Borrow tonight.

qa.q: What was Ritu thinking as she looked at the results for a long while?
qa.a: Ritu was thinking that the app had missed its whole point, since nobody could ask for a tool, and she looked disappointed but determined.

qa.q: What could Ritu do if taps stay low even after adding the button?
qa.a: Ritu could talk to a few residents about why they do not borrow, then change the next cycle's version to match.

qa.q: How might Disha see Ritu's response to the weak scores?
qa.a: Disha may be impressed that Ritu responds to what people do, as "That's evidence, not opinion" suggests.

grounding: Shows a founder adding the one feature that gives the idea its value and running two-week cycles guided by what users do.

subtype: Approach: changes one variable and measures the result [Action]
passage:
'Everyone says music helps,' Nawang said at the science club table. 'Let me check.' Sabina, the club teacher, raised an eyebrow but only asked, 'How will you know?'

Nawang had a plan. He would do twenty subtraction sums each day at the same time after lunch, at the same desk. Monday, Wednesday and Friday with earphones; Tuesday and Thursday without. He ruled a table with three columns: day, music or none, and score. By Friday it read: with music, 16, 15 and 17; without, 18 and 19.

Dolma leaned over the table. 'So no music is better?'

'For sums, this week,' said Nawang. 'One week isn't proof. Next week I'll swap the days.'

qa.q: On which days did Nawang use earphones?
qa.a: Nawang used earphones on Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

qa.q: What did Nawang want to find out?
qa.a: Nawang wanted to check whether the claim that music helps was really true, and stayed cautious, feeling one week was not proof.

qa.q: What else could Nawang change in next week's test to make it fairer?
qa.a: Nawang could swap the music days, as he plans, and keep the sums equally hard for both conditions.

qa.q: How might Dolma see the table?
qa.a: Dolma may be surprised that the result went against the popular idea, and curious about next week's swap.

grounding: Shows a student changing only music, keeping everything else the same, and recording the scores in a table over a week.
